title: How Well Does It Use Money?

cards.headline: Profit is only half the story.
cards.body: Two firms each earn **$10M**. One used **$50M** of capital to do it, the other **$500M**. The first is the far better business — it turns money into profit ten times as efficiently. Returns on capital measure exactly that skill.

cards.headline: Return on equity and assets.
cards.body: **ROE** is net income divided by shareholders' equity — profit per dollar owners put in. **ROA** divides by total assets instead, showing how well the whole asset base is used. ROA is especially telling for banks and other asset-heavy businesses.

cards.headline: A high ROE can deceive.
cards.body: Equity sits on the bottom of the ROE fraction — so debt and buybacks, which shrink equity, can lift ROE without the business improving at all. A soaring ROE beside soaring debt is a warning, not a triumph. Always read the two together.

cards.prompt: A company's ROE doubled while it piled on debt and bought back stock. Better business?
cards.explanation: Buybacks and debt reduce equity, the denominator, lifting ROE mechanically. The profit engine may be unchanged. ROIC, which counts all invested capital, is far harder to game.

cards.headline: The number hardest to fake.
cards.body: **ROIC** — after-tax operating profit over all invested capital, debt and equity together — asks how well management turns **every** dollar into operating profit. It ignores the financing tricks that flatter ROE, which is why it is the cleanest test of quality.

cards.title: Reinvesting at a high return compounds
cards.caption: A firm that reinvests at a high ROIC compounds its own value year after year — the engine behind long-term winners.

cards.body: Because it counts debt and equity together, [[1]] resists the flattery that buybacks lend to return on equity.
cards.explanation: ROIC measures return on all invested capital, so shrinking equity through buybacks doesn't inflate it the way it inflates ROE.

cards.body: Three ratios, three questions — read them together, never one alone.

cards.summary: Returns on capital reveal how efficiently a business turns money into profit.
bullets: ROE is profit per dollar of equity; ROA per dollar of assets.
Debt and buybacks can inflate ROE without real improvement.
ROIC is the cleanest, hardest-to-game quality test.

cards.insight: A great business reinvests at high returns and compounds. A weak one burns capital just to stand still.
